title: Faith in mind
hook: a Chan poem attributed to the third patriarch Sengcan: the great way is not hard for those without picking and choosing

segments.voice: Yesterday, shikantaza: just sitting, with no object at all, the way Dogen taught it. Your line: just this. Was there one moment yesterday that got to be just this? Day one thousand two hundred twelve.

The great way is not difficult. That is how the poem opens, and for half a line it sounds like very good news. Then comes the condition. It is not difficult for those who don't pick and choose. Which can describe a whole morning. Coffee or tea. Skip this song. That email can wait, this one can't. Left lane or right. The poem is short and plain, built from paired lines that sound almost like proverbs, and some Chan and Zen students chant it and carry it. Tradition credits it to Sengcan, remembered in the Chan lineage as the third ancestor, counting Bodhidharma as the first. Today: faith in mind.
screen: `THE GREAT WAY IS NOT DIFFICULT.` → `EXCEPT FOR ONE THING.` → `A POEM CARRIED BY CHAN.`

segments.voice: First, the title. In Chinese it is Xinxin Ming, often given in English as Faith in Mind, or Trust in Mind. The two words read xin are different words. The first means trust or faith. The second means heart-mind, the whole of what thinks and feels. So the faith here is not faith in a creed. Some readers hear it as trust that the mind, as it is, is already enough to meet the way. Second, the condition. In paraphrase, the poem goes on: when love and hate are both absent, everything becomes clear and open. The way is not hidden. Something is standing in front of it, and the poem names it as the habit of grabbing at one side and pushing away the other. Third, the poem does not say stop having taste. You can still notice that the tea is too strong. What it calls the sickness of the mind is setting what you like against what you dislike, turning every small preference into a quiet war. Rain on the day of a picnic is rain. The poem's interest is in everything that gets piled on top of the rain. Fourth, why it is called faith. The poem describes the way as round and complete, like vast space, with nothing lacking and nothing extra. It is only because we take and reject, it says, that we don't see it so. Yesterday's practice, just sitting, is this same trust done with the body: no target, no improvement project, just this. The poem is that trust put into words.
screen: `THE TITLE: FAITH IN MIND.` · `NOT HIDDEN, JUST BLOCKED.` · `TASTE IS FINE; THE WAR IS NOT.` · `ROUND AND COMPLETE, LIKE SPACE.` · then, large: `NO PICKING AND CHOOSING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like to try it. Sit comfortably and let the breath find its own pace. For this sit, take what the body brings. An itch on the cheek, a stiff knee, cool air on the hands. Each one may come with an urge attached: scratch it, shift, fix it. You don't need to obey the urge or fight it. See it as a preference, and let the sensation be a sensation for a few breaths. If you do need to move, move slowly, knowing you chose. Then, before the bell, choose one small preference you'll set down later today: which seat, which song, which line at the store. Let it go in advance. The bell holds the time.
Xinxin Ming. The Chan poem whose title is often rendered Faith in Mind, and which opens: the great way is not difficult for those who don't pick and choose. Today's word.
Your line: no picking and choosing. Today, drop one small preference and take what comes, just once, on purpose. Day one thousand two hundred twelve.

howItsDone: In some Zen and Chan communities the Xinxin Ming is chanted or recited in services and studied in talks, and students often learn its opening lines by heart.

fork.setup: it rains on the day you planned a picnic, and the poem's first line comes to mind. what is the poem pointing at?
options: the rain, and the fight piled on top of it
pretend you wanted rain all along
fork.reveal: the poem doesn't ask you to fake a preference. it points at the war between liking and disliking, the thing piled on top of the rain.

notes: All poem lines are paraphrased; no public-domain English translation on the approved list was used, so nothing is in quotation marks.
Attribution to Sengcan is given as tradition's. Keeper to decide whether to mention that the attribution is questioned; the script does not.
Check the glosses: 信 as trust/faith, 心 as heart-mind; 'sickness of the mind' for setting like against dislike; 'round and complete like vast space, nothing lacking, nothing extra'.
'Third ancestor, counting Bodhidharma as the first' is framed as how the Chan lineage remembers him (Bodhidharma, Huike, Sengcan).
Pronunciation 'shin-shin-MING' approximates Mandarin xìn xīn míng.

Editor pass: fixed the lineage count (third ancestor counting Bodhidharma as first, not 'after' him); softened 'Chan and Zen students chant it' and 'many communities' to 'some'; cut the stock 'this is easy to miss'; replaced the sounds-and-tags practice (too close to day 1202's listening practice) with a body-sensation version of the same no-picking idea.
